newsitem.title: USA: What's a dollar worth today? Ask the Minneapolis Fed.
newsitem.headline: What's a dollar worth today? Ask the Minneapolis Fed.

text.p: You're probably making more money now than you were, say, 10 years ago. But are you really?

The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis has an answer for you, and it's online. The bank's Web site is offering a new online calculator that will adjust any dollar amount for inflation during the years from 1913 to 1997.

Just punch in the numbers and dates and the answer will flash on your screen in a few seconds. Take a U.S. worker whose annual salary was $30,000 in 1980. That same worker would have to earn $58,799 today to make up for inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index over that period.
Inflation occurs when prices rise over a sustained period of time, which decreases the purchasing power of money.

The calculator was developed by economists and the public affairs department of the Minneapolis Fed, one of the Federal Reserve's 12 regional banks, to respond to the growing number of questions the department receives about inflation.
"There are so many people who call us wondering what this product that they bought in 1960 or 1950 is worth in today's dollars," Minneapolis Fed analyst Rob Grunewald said.
But the Web site's audience is even broader.

Grunewald said lawyers in charge of people's estates are constantly looking for inflation-adjusted numbers to compare how much a deed or real estate would be worth in today's dollars. Even schools are using the service.
The Minneapolis Fed analyst said he has received e-mail from teachers who said they were planning to use the site as part of their students' homework assigments.
"What I don't know is if the students are cringing or glad to have this on the Internet," Grunewald quipped.

The Minneapolis Fed's new calculator is being offered with inflation remarkably subdued. Consumer prices rose at just a 1.4 percent rate in the first half of 1997, the slowest rate in 11 years, the government said Wednesday. The Consumer Price Index, the government's main inflation gauge, rose 3.3 percent for all of 1996.
The CPI, compiled monthly by the Bureau of Labour Statistics, is meant to measure price changes for a basket of goods and services bought by American consumers.

Grunewald said the new calculator does not work well with versions of Windows 3.11 or earlier Windows releases. It works with Java Script-based browsers, but Netscape browser versions 2.0 or higher will provide the best results, he said.
The Minneapolis Fed site can be found on the World Wide Web at http://woodrow.mpls.frb.fed.us/economy/calc/cpihome.html.
